job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Marco Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now my day is the job site and the shelves. I get up at seven, sit at the kitchen table in the flat I share with my mum and little sister in Harbourgate, and send three or four applications. I did accounting with a good result and eight weeks at Dunmore Payroll, a small bureau, but no offer has come. In the afternoon I stack shelves at the supermarket three days a week, and I'm tired of being told I did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say good, maybe the hype dies and the graduate jobs stop vanishing. At the pub I'd tell my mates the big banks only blame robots to hide that they won't pay for juniors. Online I wouldn't bother, I barely post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes for me, and that's the problem. I've sent about sixty applications since June and got two rejections and silence from the rest. My student loan statement arrives every month like a bill for a promise that never came true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, ten a week, to payroll bureaus and council finance teams around Harbourgate. I'd ask the university careers office to look at my CV again, and I'd take more shelf-stacking hours to cover my share of the rent to my mum. I wouldn't spend on courses I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stuck, mostly. I got a good result, I did the internship, and I'm still refreshing my email at seven in the morning. It makes me feel like a number the market has already decided not to hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Then what would you want the big banks to do instead of blaming robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hire juniors and train them, the way they used to. A big firm could pay one fewer director and train twenty graduates, and nobody would notice the difference. I'd even like a rule that firms over a certain size must take on trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill gets squeezed first if the shelf-stacking hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone contract goes first, then the takeaway on Fridays. I'd tell my mum honestly if I can't give her the electricity share. The loan payment comes straight out of pay once I earn over the threshold, so I can't skip that anyway.

say: I'd say the **hype** will fade and graduate jobs should come back.
I'd tell my mates the big banks **blame robots** to dodge training juniors.
think: Nothing changes, and that is **the problem**: sixty applications since June, almost no replies.
My **loan** statement feels like a bill for a promise that never came true.
do: Send **ten applications** a week to payroll bureaus and council finance teams near Harbourgate.
Take extra **shelf-stacking** shifts to pay my share of the rent to my mum.
Ask the careers office to **rework** my CV.
feel: **Stuck**, and tired of being told he did everything right.
S0.quote: A big firm could pay one fewer director and train twenty graduates, and nobody would notice the difference.
fieldNote: **Anger** at big firms, not at technology, drives his view.
Describes a clear **plan** but little hope it will work; he has no cushion at all.
Supports a **rule** making large firms take trainees, in line with his union-friendly views.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to payroll bureaus and council finance teams
Take extra shelf-stacking shifts to cover rent at home
Drop the phone contract and the Friday takeaway
Ask the university careers office to rework the CV

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I feared: the entry jobs are the checking and data entry that software takes first. At the pub I'd tell my mates this is a choice by firms to save money, not nature. I'd say the government should protect people the way it protects farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It scares me, because the jobs I'm applying for are exactly the checking and bookkeeping tasks on that list. Dunmore Payroll (where I interned) told me they won't replace a junior who left in spring. I don't use any AI tools, and I feel the gap growing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shelf-stacking, apply wider, even to warehouse office roles, and finally do one free spreadsheet course at the library. I'd go to the union meeting my aunt keeps asking me to, because someone has to speak for people like me. I'd try AI tools only if I'm forced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry first, then tired. It feels like the ladder was pulled up just as I reached the bottom rung. My stomach tightens when I open the job site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try AI tools only if forced. What's holding you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust it, and I'm slow with new software. I once spent a week learning the payroll package at my internship and still made errors. If someone showed me for an hour in person, not a video, I might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger sister, who starts college next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister not to borrow for a business degree unless the course has a guaranteed placement. I'd say look at something with hands in it, like nursing or electrics. It hurts, because I always told her to study what she loves, but loving it doesn't pay the loan.

say: I'd say firms are **choosing** to cut juniors to save money.
I'd push the government to **protect** people the way it protects farmers.
think: Checking and bookkeeping are the **exact tasks** I'm applying for, and they go first.
Dunmore Payroll won't replace a **junior** who left, and I don't use AI.
do: Apply **wider**, even to warehouse office jobs.
Finish one free **spreadsheet** course at the library.
Go to the **union** meeting my aunt keeps inviting me to.
feel: **Angry** first, then tired, as if the ladder was pulled up.
My stomach **tightens** when I open the job site.
S1.quote: I'd tell my sister not to borrow for a business degree unless the course has a guaranteed placement.
fieldNote: Sees the change as a **political choice** by firms, which matches his left-leaning outlook.
**Resistant** to AI tools, and says so, but would learn from a person in the room.
**Worry** spreads to his sister's future, not only his own.

steps.text: Apply for warehouse office and admin roles as well as accounts
Finish one free spreadsheet course at the library
Go to the union branch meeting his aunt keeps mentioning
Keep the supermarket shifts while the search continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say governments need to act now: a basic income, shorter weeks, retraining paid for by the companies that profit. Two years is nothing. I'd march if somebody organised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm finished before I start. By 2028 I'm 25, still paying off the loan, and the junior accounting work is gone. I have no savings and nobody in my family can catch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd put every spare pound against the loan and join the union's youth branch. I'd ask my mum to let me pay less rent for a while, which I'd hate. I'd take any job at all, even night shifts, before everyone's fighting for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit numb. I picture my mum's face when I tell her it was all for nothing. I can't see a plan, only a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marching. Who would you be marching against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not against the AI itself. Against the handful of owners who'd collect all the money from it. I'd want a tax on the machines' profits that pays everyone, and I'd say it loudly at my union branch. I don't know if it's realistic, but silence is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. Does that change the shelf-stacking plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. The supermarket already has self-checkouts, and a stacking robot is the obvious next step. So night shifts are a bridge of three years, not a career. That's grim, because there's no safe floor underneath me.

say: I'd demand a **basic income** and retraining paid for by the firms that profit.
I'd march if a **union** organised it, because two years is nothing.
think: I'm **finished** before I start: 25, still in debt, and junior accounting work gone.
I have **no savings** and no family safety net.
do: Put every spare pound against the **loan** and join the union youth branch.
Ask my mum to cut my **rent** for a while.
Take any **night-shift** job before everyone is fighting for them.
feel: **Scared** and a little numb, with a clock but no plan.
S2.quote: By 2028 I'm 25, still paying off the loan, and the junior accounting work is gone.
fieldNote: Expects to lose the whole **entry-level** route and sees no fallback.
Turns fear into **politics**: wants a tax on AI profits and a union voice.
Understands that **robots** will soon reach even supermarket shelves, so his bridge job is short.

steps.text: Join the union youth branch and go to the first march
Put every spare pound against the student loan
Ask mum to lower his rent share for a while
Take any night-shift job to keep money coming in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a proper plan if governments start now. If I had a workplace, I'd push the union to bargain over AI before it arrives. Online I'd share anything that argues for retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a real chance to land a job and then be the one they keep. But I know I'd be tempted to stick my head in the sand with the tech. My fear is that by 2031 I've got three years of experience in a job that no longer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any payroll or accounts-assistant job this year, even at low pay, to build experience. In the evenings I'd learn the AI payroll tools so I'm not the one they let go. I'd keep paying the loan down and join the union, because a contract in my name matters more than my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. There's a little hope because five years is long, but also a heavy feeling, like waiting for a test result. Most of me just wants to get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you learn the tools, when you've avoided them so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reason I can see, like a manager saying learn this or lose your seat. Left alone I'd drift, and I'm honest that I need pressure. At Dunmore Payroll a colleague called Pat taught me one spreadsheet macro and it felt great, so a person next to me works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And how does your mum, who you live with, fit into a five-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum cleans offices at night and her knees are going. A steady wage by 2031 would let her cut hours. If I fail, my mum keeps cleaning offices into her sixties, and that's what really keeps me up at night.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** for a plan if governments start now.
I'd push the union to **bargain** over AI before it arrives.
think: Five years could let me **land a job** and be the one they keep.
I fear three years of experience in a job that **no longer exists**.
do: Take any payroll or **accounts-assistant** job this year, even at low pay.
Learn the **AI payroll** tools in the evenings.
Keep paying the **loan** down and join the union.
feel: **Mixed**: a little hope, and a heavy feeling like waiting for a test result.
S3.quote: If I fail, my mum keeps cleaning offices into her sixties, and that's what really keeps me up at night.
fieldNote: His **mother's** night cleaning job and sore knees make his own success a family matter.
Admits he needs **outside pressure** outside pressure to learn new tools, and that a person beside him works best.
Five years gives him a **plan** him a plan, but he still expects his income to be at risk.

steps.text: Take any payroll or accounts-assistant job within the year
Learn the AI payroll tools in the evenings
Join the union and ask about bargaining over AI
Keep paying the loan down faster than required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is generous. I'd say let's use it: free retraining, apprenticeships in finance work, and rules so firms can't dump workers overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, ten years means I could build a whole career and still be pushed out at 33. But my loan would be mostly gone and my mum retired by then. That's a cushion I don't have in the faster ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in accounting and aim for a chartered qualification, one exam at a time, paid by whichever employer takes me. Alongside it I'd learn a bit of the AI tools each year, slowly. And I'd vote for whoever promises real training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. Ten years feels like a long road with fog at the end, but at least it's a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer time change what you'd tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd say go ahead with the degree but pick an area that deals with people, like advising families on money, and keep a second skill in your pocket. With ten years she can adjust, with two she couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from what you're doing today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting to be rescued by a job posting. I'd volunteer as a treasurer for a local charity, build a name, and learn their software on their time. I wasted months being angry when I could have been collecting references.

say: I'd say use the decade for **free retraining** and finance apprenticeships.
I'd back rules so firms can't **dump workers** overnight.
think: I could build a whole career and still be **pushed out** at 33.
Ten years means the **loan** is mostly paid and my mum is retired.
do: Study for a **chartered** accounting qualification, one exam at a time.
Learn a little of the **AI tools** each year.
Volunteer as a charity **treasurer** to collect references.
feel: **Uneasy** but steadier: a long road with fog at the end.
S4.quote: I wasted months being angry when I could have been collecting references.
fieldNote: The **longer timeline** softens his anger and lets him plan.
Wants a **second skill** and a human-facing niche rather than trusting one job to last.
Admits his **own part** in standing still, which is rare in his other answers.

steps.text: Start one chartered accounting exam paper with an employer's help
Volunteer as treasurer for a local charity
Learn one new AI tool each year at a slow pace
Vote for parties that promise paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The Plateau worries me least on paper, yet it's my life right now, so it's a strange answer. The one that scares me most is 2028, because two years doesn't let my debt shrink or my mum retire. What would help is a guaranteed trainee place in a real finance job, a pause on loan payments while I'm out of work, and someone to show me the new tools in person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't lazy and aren't asking for handouts. We did the degree, we did the internship, and we want to be told where to turn up on Monday.

headlineQuote: We did the degree, we did the internship, and we want to be told where to turn up on Monday.
portrait: Marco, 23, has a **good accounting degree**, one short internship and a loan he can't touch, living with his mum and sister.
He blames **big firms and banks** more than technology, and wants unions, rules and training places.
He avoids AI tools and fears the **gap widening**, though he would learn from a person in the room.
His mood stays **anxious** to alarmed because he has no savings and his mother's wage is already stretched.
More time helps him plan, but he never feels the **plan is safe**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most: two years won't let his debt shrink or his mother retire.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **trainee place**, a pause on loan payments, and someone showing him the new tools **in person**.
